The Browns are building a stadium in Brook Park and expanding their headquarters in Berea. In neighboring Middleburg Heights, the mayor is asking what game-day traffic will mean for roads that already back up, and who will pay for any extra police and fire coverage.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b682f0ff-e69c-40d3-86a8-641ce00fc9a1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Those were among the questions at the Nov. 18 America 250 mayors' panel at Baldwin Wallace University. University President Lee Fisher moderated the discussion with Berea Mayor Cyril Kleem, Brook Park Mayor Edward Orcutt and Middleburg Heights Mayor Matt Castelli. [bereachamberofcommerce.wildapricot.org](https://substack.com/redirect/444c37d2-cabd-4f27-9506-3f75eee22b95?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..c7Q-kELjeZUpoNEk63mHYUVdnfKy9Z6XhOWR1Gdp4CQ?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=225716785)
_The panel discussion has been condensed and paraphrased for clarity._
_[See full transcript here](https://substack.com/redirect/97f7f53f-8bb1-4b94-9c60-13e9150487fb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) (note: I have recording issues so a bit of the beginning and end is cut off)_
* * *
**Lee Fisher:** As we celebrate the country's 250th anniversary, what part of your city's history helps explain the place it is today?
**Cyril Kleem, Berea:** John Baldwin is the link between the university and the city. After farming didn't work out for him, he developed the sandstone industry. People came here from different countries to work in it, and that helped make Berea a diverse community. A lot of Berea was already built before World War II, earlier than many suburbs. We have historic neighborhoods people love, and we also have streets and infrastructure that cost more to maintain because they're that old.
**Edward Orcutt, Brook Park:** Ford brought thousands of jobs here after World War II. Homes went up, other industries came in to support Ford, and families stayed for generations. What the city did with that industrial tax base was important, too. It invested in recreation and parks where people could come together. My oldest son is buying a house across the street from us. I think he likes his mom's cooking.
**Matt Castelli, Middleburg Heights:** There's an onion in the middle of our city seal. The soil around Lake Abram was rich enough to grow onions and garlic, and growers shipped onions across the country. Later, Ford helped drive residential growth here, and Southland became a major shopping district. It's still going today. We've been working to keep it viable for another generation, including bringing Meijer to the former Sears site.
* * *
**Lee Fisher:** What's your biggest challenge as mayor, and where do you see the most opportunity?
**Matt Castelli:** Municipal income tax is our main source of revenue, so attracting investment is how we keep paying for services. In a built-up city, you have to figure out what to do with land that's already been used for something else. At Southland, we had multiple owners going in different directions. We had people proposing self-storage or a lumberyard. The city had to lay out what it wanted for the district. Before redevelopment, the properties I'm talking about brought in about $48,000. We expect more than $600,000 a year afterward. That kind of change helps pay for things like stormwater improvements that older suburbs need.
**Edward Orcutt:** Infrastructure is a big one. So is explaining to people why something is a priority. On social media, the first person to post can set the narrative. By the time you come back with facts, people may have made up their minds. We have to listen to residents, tell them what we can afford and explain how we decided what comes first.
**Cyril Kleem:** Redevelopment is difficult when you're trying to maintain the character of an older city. Political division also makes it harder to get things done. And the three of us recently met about mental health. Our police, fire and social services departments are dealing with it firsthand. We're trying to work together with the hospital and other local resources because we're seeing more people become isolated.
* * *
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b9cdde1f-4978-4c1d-84f3-32f620b1b354?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
From right to left, Baldwin Wallace University President Lee Fisher, Berea Mayor Cyril Kleem, Brook Park Mayor Ed Orcutt, and Middleburg Heights Mayor Matt Castelli.
**Lee Fisher:** The Browns are moving their stadium to Brook Park. What made the city think it could handle a project that big?
**Edward Orcutt:** We had 177 acres we'd been looking to redevelop for years. We looked at the roads, the interstates, the turnpike and the RTA station. Ford used to bring thousands of workers in and out of that area, so we knew what the site had handled before. The stadium gives us a chance to bring in year-round activity, with events, apartments, hotels, restaurants and retail. When you look at what the Browns are doing in Berea, what's happening at the airport and what could happen at the I-X Center, you can see how those projects connect.
* * *
**Lee Fisher:** What's happening with the Browns' development in Berea?
**Cyril Kleem:** I first approached the Browns in 2009 about whether they wanted to stay and whether they wanted a new facility. Years later, they came back with an interest in expanding around their existing location. We committed to acquiring those properties without eminent domain. The Browns had to make individual offers, and that took time.
The project includes an expansion of the training facility, a hotel, apartments, sports medicine and a community football field where our high school team can play. The city didn't put money into the project upfront, and we were paid for city-owned property. Keeping the Browns here is important because they're our largest income taxpayer.
* * *
**Lee Fisher:** How does the new stadium affect Middleburg Heights?
**Matt Castelli:** We get the traffic (joke). We've had good conversations with Brook Park and the Browns, and we asked the regional planning agency, NOACA, to look beyond the improvements around Snow Road. What happens at Bagley and Engle? What happens in Berea, Parma and Fairview Park? The additional studies identified six other areas where we should look at improvements.
There's going to be congestion. We need to figure out how to limit it, what road improvements will be needed and how we'll pay for any additional police and fire coverage. Those are conversations I want to have with the state, because the effects cross city lines.
* * *
**Lee Fisher:** How do you bring in investment while protecting the neighborhoods people moved there for?
**Cyril Kleem:** The Browns wanted a street connection left open for access. We decided it should close once construction is finished because of what traffic could do to the neighborhood. On a separate townhouse project, we could have built about 40 percent more units. We kept it smaller to preserve green space and limit the impact on neighbors and city services. We also turned down a proposed annexation twice because of traffic and sewer concerns. More tax revenue is one part of the decision. You have to look at what the public will have to live with and pay for.
**Edward Orcutt:** We're looking at traffic signals that can adjust based on how many cars are coming through. On major event days, that could help keep cars moving where traffic is backing up. And if the development brings in the revenue we expect, I want to put it back into things residents already use, like parks and playgrounds.
**Matt Castelli:** We've set aside more than 80 acres for green space over the last five years. Our goal is for every home to be within a 10-minute walk of a park or green space. We've gotten more than halfway there. When a piece of property becomes available, sometimes the best use is to preserve it.
* * *
**Lee Fisher:** What do you hope your city looks like 15 years from now?
**Cyril Kleem:** I want Baldwin Wallace here and healthy, and I expect the Browns will still be here. I can see cities doing more purchasing together and sharing information more easily. I don't expect us to merge. I also think policing will keep changing. Recruiting officers has gotten harder, and we're doing more with technology, community policing, mental health response and de-escalation.
**Edward Orcutt:** I'd like to see a Super Bowl in Ohio. And I hope whoever is running Brook Park then manages the city's money well and keeps public safety first. I've lived here for 30 years. I want to keep living in a place where people feel safe.
**Matt Castelli:** I think Lake Erie and our Metroparks will become more valuable to people deciding where to live. We have freshwater and a trail system we can keep connecting across communities. I'd also like people to put down their phones a little more and check in on the neighbor who lives alone.
* * *
**Audience member:** How are the three cities handling AI?
**Cyril Kleem:** My biggest technology concern is security, particularly because Berea operates its own water plant. We've trained staff and discussed cybersecurity with council. Some of those discussions happen in executive session because we don't want to make the details of our defenses public.
**Matt Castelli:** AI could make city operations more efficient, but if employers use it to replace workers, cities stand to lose income tax revenue. I'd like to see a discussion about whether companies should pay a tax when they use AI to eliminate jobs. Otherwise, the people who lose their jobs could end up paying more for local services. With data centers, we also need to think about where they go and what their environmental impact will be.
**Edward Orcutt:** If a company wants to build a data center, ask how it will cool the facility and who will pay for the electrical upgrades. Depending on the design, closed-loop cooling can reduce the need to draw water from local supplies. And I'd tell companies they have to pay for the infrastructure they need. A developer can walk in with a sweet deal on paper, and you can have a ribbon cutting. The question is what the town is left with ten years later.
* * *
Thank you to Berea Mayor Cyril Kleem, Brook Park Mayor Edward Orcutt and Middleburg Heights Mayor Matt Castelli for taking the time to talk about what's ahead for their cities. Thanks also to Baldwin Wallace University President Lee Fisher for moderating the panel and to Berea Ward 4 Councilwoman Erika Coble for putting the event together and taking questions from the audience.

#
# **Thank You to Our Community for Joining the Philly Reads Literacy Summit!**
_Saturday was an unforgettable morning of community action_
* * *
On Saturday, November 14, hundreds of Philadelphia students, parents, adult learners, educators, and community leaders gathered at the School of the Future for the first [Philly Reads Literacy Summit](http://enews.senatorhughes.com/mail/util.cfm?mailaction=clickthru&gpiv=2100172768.172186.5&gen=1&mailing_linkid=19094). Grounded in our mission to [LEARN, CONNECT, and ACT](http://enews.senatorhughes.com/mail/util.cfm?mailaction=clickthru&gpiv=2100172768.172186.5&gen=1&mailing_linkid=19095), we came together to address Philadelphia's literacy crisis head-on and put real, practical resources directly into the hands of families and schools.
* * *
**Highlights from the Summit**
* **Practical Tools for Families: **Parents and caregivers joined hands-on workshops to learn how to build stronger reading habits at home and turn classroom insights into everyday action.

* **Youth Voices Leading the Way** : K-12 students took part in grade-specific literacy labs and youth panels, sharing honest perspectives on what motivates them to read and how our city can better support young learners.

* **Educator & Adult Learner Support: **Teachers participated in dedicated professional learning sessions and explored resources tailored to structured literacy and lifelong learning.

* **Health, Literacy, and Career Resources: **Alongside literacy programming, families accessed free children's health screenings and direct support from more than 20 local community organizations.

* * *
**"Cities across the country, including Philadelphia, are facing a literacy crisis that can only be solved when the entire community comes to the table. On Saturday, we moved beyond conversation and provided practical, evidence-based tools directly to our neighbors. We need to take the power into our own hands. If we don 't lead the charge on this issue, we can't expect anyone else to."** **-_Senator Vincent Hughes_**
* * *
[**VIEW SUMMIT PHOTOS AND A RECAP HERE **](http://enews.senatorhughes.com/mail/util.cfm?mailaction=clickthru&gpiv=2100172768.172186.5&gen=1&mailing_linkid=19096)
* * *
**We Want to Hear from You! ** Whether you attended Saturday's summit or are passionate about strengthening literacy in your neighborhood, your voice helps shape what we build next. **[TAKE THE 2 MINUTE SURVEY](http://enews.senatorhughes.com/mail/util.cfm?mailaction=clickthru&gpiv=2100172768.172186.5&gen=1&mailing_linkid=19096)**
* * *

Hey folks,
While millions of Americans were left stranded at airports, Trump's Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin decides it was a great time to hop on a government jet and watch college football.
I wish I were kidding.
This one is personal for me. I got caught in the travel chaos myself and missed precious time with my son. But what really gets me is how little these people seem to care. And now, even some of MAGA's biggest defenders are turning on Mullin.
* [**00:01:34**] Mullin's private jet scandal unfolds as widespread FAA disruptions leave Americans stranded. I share how the chaos kept me from seeing my son and why this is about more than one football game.
* [**00:04:22**] The contractor connection raises serious questions. Mullin reportedly spends part of the game in a luxury box belonging to the CEO of a company with DHS contracts. How is this acceptable?
* [**00:07:06**] Mullin tries to explain the technology failures, but his answers only create more confusion. We dig into the questions surrounding FAA upgrades, AI, government contracts, and Sean Duffy's handling of the crisis.
* [**00:11:00**] Even MAGA media is turning on him. Megyn Kelly says she has zero confidence in Mullin, while conservative commentator Todd Starnes goes further and calls for his resignation.
* [**00:13:37**] The political backlash is getting bigger. We talk about growing frustration with Trump's administration, the election warning signs Republicans can't ignore, and why Americans deserve leaders who actually know how to govern.

Here's what makes me so angry about all of this: Government is supposed to work for us. It's supposed to keep people safe, solve problems, and make our lives a little easier. Instead, we're watching officials dodge accountability while ordinary Americans pay the price.
And when even Trump's own media allies start calling out the incompetence, we need to pay attention.
This episode is about the FAA travel disaster, Mullin's private jet controversy, and a much bigger failure of leadership inside the Trump administration. It's about what happens when loyalty matters more than competence and the people in charge forget who they're supposed to serve.
**We deserve better. And we can 't afford to look away.**
That's why I'm building Endless Urgency. Not to give powerful people another platform for excuses, but to ask the hard questions, expose the hypocrisy, and make sure the people affected by these decisions aren't forgotten.

Anyone who’s spent time on the water in Hampton Roads knows that the tide always turns.
Four years ago, I lost this seat. I didn’t second-guess the fight then, and I’m glad I didn’t.
On November 3rd, the tide turned.
The people of Hampton Roads sent me back to Congress. And we weren’t alone. Across the country, voters delivered a blue wave that flipped the House with what’s on track to be the largest Democratic majority in decades. Democrats flipped Senate seats in places like Kansas, Texas, and Ohio to take back that chamber too.
All cycle, I said Democrats needed to flip just three House seats to take back the majority. We blew right past that number, and VA-02 was one of the seats that got us there.
I’m proud of that. I’m also not one to oversell, so here’s the plain truth about how we did it:
We spent down to zero.
When you’re in a Toss-Up race against an incumbent and a flood of outside money, you don’t hold anything in reserve. You leave it all on the deck.
Every dollar went into this victory. That was the right call. But it means that before I’m sworn in, we need to settle up.

Friend, Last night, as one of their first acts in the lame duck session of Congress, the Senate passed a so-called permitting reform bill that is a huge handout to Big Oil and Big Tech. This bill strips away what little tools our communities have to defend ourselves from corporate polluters. It threatens Tribal Nations, sacred sites, and important laws like the Clean Water Act. It would speed up construction of data centers and make it easier for fracked gas pipelines. Growing up in Southwest Detroit, I know all too well what it feels like to be invisible to all levels of government ― watching corporate polluters poison our air and water. clean_body: We have the right to challenge data centers in our communities. But not if this disastrous bill passes >> | | | Friend, Last night, as one of their first acts in the lame duck session of Congress, the Senate passed a so-called permitting reform bill that is a huge handout to Big Oil and Big Tech. This bill strips away what little tools our communities have to defend ourselves from corporate polluters. It threatens Tribal Nations, sacred sites, and important laws like the Clean Water Act. It would speed up construction of data centers and make it easier for fracked gas pipelines. Growing up in Southwest Detroit, I know all too well what it feels like to be invisible to all levels of government ― watching corporate polluters poison our air and water. | This bill is 417 pages of bad ideas and empty promises, written in secrecy without public input. According to Friends of the Earth, “The horror is that [the permitting reform bill] goes above and beyond what the far-right brain trust dreamt up in Project 2025.”1 But together, we're going to out-organize them and demand Congress reject this horrible permitting bill. Please see my message from earlier this week below for more details. In solidarity, Rashida 1 \---------- Forwarded message --------- From: Rashida Tlaib** Date: Wed, Nov 18, 2026 Subject: If this bill passes, Big Tech could be building data centers on Native sacred sites To: dpwillis67@gmail.com Friend, Democrats and Republicans in the Senate are claiming that Congress needs to pass the so-called Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act now, before the new Congress is sworn in in January. But this bill is more than 400 pages of bad ideas and empty promises. It’s a gift to Big Oil and Big Tech, and would super-charge fossil fuel and data center construction in our communities. This week, the Senate cleared the last procedural hurdle and could vote on this bill before Thanksgiving. Together with my colleagues Reps. Adelita Grijalva (AZ), Summer Lee (PA), and Melanie Stansbury (NM), I’m leading the effort to stop this dangerous bill that would allow unaccountable, greedy corporations to speed up data center and fracked natural gas pipeline construction. This bill makes it easier to build fossil fuel infrastructure while undermining clean water and national environmental policy acts. It would also strip away Tribes’ and the general public’s right to give input and sue to stop polluting projects and to protect culturally significant areas. Too often, we’re seeing local and state elected officials enter into non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with Big Tech over the construction of AI data centers ― hiding potential environmental impacts, harms to public health, and tax break packages for billion-dollar corporations. That’s why I’ve introduced the No Secret Deals Act to prohibit public officials and government agencies from entering into NDAs and hiding the true impacts of data centers on our communities. Growing up in southwest Detroit by the Marathon Oil Refinery and other corporate polluters, I know what it’s like to live in a frontline community treated as a sacrifice zone. I will not stand by and watch as corporate polluters poison our air and water. With you in the fight for better, Rashida * Rashida Tlaib for Congress PO Box 32777 Detroit, MI 48232 | Paid for by Rashida Tlaib for Congress | | Sent via . name: Wes Moore
subject: A conversation
body:
# [](https://act.wesmoore.com/go/8?t=1&akid=2318%2E1086043%2E2RmuLI)
This summer, I sat down for Jubilee’s _Surrounded_ and debated with 20 people who had not voted in the last election.
**The cynics out there in the world tell us a conversation like the one I had isn’t worth having.** That we’ve become too divided. That everyone has already chosen a side, and the only thing left to do is shout louder than our political opponents.
But that isn’t what I saw in that room. And I do not think it is true in this country. We haven’t crossed a threshold where we can no longer listen to one another or to work together.
The year that we celebrated America’s 250th anniversary, I’m struck by the fact that our nation’s story has never been one of perfection. It’s one of progress. Generation after generation, Americans have chosen to do their part in expanding the promise of this country.
That work has never been automatic. It has always required participation from people who believe that tomorrow can be better than today.
**[If you share that belief with me, I would appreciate a donation today so we can continue our work.](https://act.wesmoore.com/go/417?c0=wes-em-20261120-1.cJZPH1&refcode=em-20261120-1&t=2&akid=2318%2E1086043%2E2RmuLI)**
I did not go into _Surrounded_ – or write this – to shame people who have opted out of the system.
Quite the contrary. I understand that choice.
I don’t come from a political background. When I ran for office the first time a few years ago, I had to convince many of my family members to vote for me. It’s not like we aren’t cool. They just don’t rush to the ballot box every year.
It struck me that people I love – people who cared deeply about their communities and their country – had been absent from a democratic act that generations of Americans fought for.
Somewhere along the way, they stopped believing that politics had much to do with them – or that anyone in politics had much interest in them. That realization has stayed with me. And it is exactly why I did _Surrounded._
Democracy is a relationship. Those who have the privilege of serving in government share a responsibility to give people a reason to believe their participation counts. To earn their trust. To show the public that government is not something that happens to us, but something we have the power to shape. As an elected official, I take that responsibility seriously. It’s sacred, and essential.
If those of us in public office do our jobs right, then voting becomes about more than casting a ballot. It is an act of hope.
If we’re serious about strengthening democracy over the next 250 years, we cannot only invest in elections. _We have to invest in one another._ The work of patriotism is not passive, and it is not performative. It is service.
Real patriotism asks us to see our humanity in each other before we see our differences. It asks us to remember that the future of this country has always depended on ordinary people doing extraordinary things together – not because they agreed on everything, but because they believed this nation was worth building together, despite our disagreements.
**[If you’re with me, and you believe in what we’re building together, can you chip in any amount to support our work today?](https://act.wesmoore.com/go/417?c0=wes-em-20261120-1.cJZPH1&refcode=em-20261120-1&t=3&akid=2318%2E1086043%2E2RmuLI)**
My final challenge is a simple one: Sit down with people in your life and in your community who disagree with you. Have honest conversations. Listen. You may be surprised by what you find. And you may even end up working together to make a big difference in our world.
Elevate,
Wes
[ ](https://act.wesmoore.com/go/417?c0=wes-em-20261120-1.cJZPH1&refcode=em-20261120-1&t=4&akid=2318%2E1086043%2E2RmuLI)

* * *
**[Donate »](https://secure.actblue.com/donate/wes-em-footer?refcode=em-20261120-1&t=5&refcode2=2318_1086043_2RmuLI&akid=2318%2E1086043%2E2RmuLI)**
**[Volunteer »](https://support.wesmoore.com/a/volunteer?source=em-20261120-1)**
This email was sent to dpwillis67@gmail.com. Email is a critical way we communicate with grassroots supporters like you. However, if you would like to change your subscription preferences, here are some options:
* [Receive Fewer Emails](https://act.wesmoore.com/signup/receive-fewer-emails/?t=6&akid=2318%2E1086043%2E2RmuLI)

Hi Peter, it's Ellen — founder of EMILYs List.
When I started EMILYs List in 1985, I had a simple idea: If we could bring together enough people willing to invest in Democratic pro-choice women _early_ , we could change the face of political power in America.
Forty one years later, I think it's fair to say we were onto something.
Just look at what happened this November: Democratic pro-choice women helped take back the U.S. House and Senate. They won historic governors' races, flipped Republican-held seats, and broke barriers that once seemed impossible to overcome.
**These victories didn't happen by accident. They happened because we built a movement that believed in women, invested in them, and stood by them long before anyone knew their names.**
That's what EMILYs List has always been about. And it's why I'm writing to you today.

Back in the early days of EMILYs List, I used to talk a lot about the importance of _winning today and building for tomorrow_. That belief is still core to EMILYs List's mission.
**The work we did over the past four decades helped change the direction of this country in 2026. And the investments we make today could shape American politics for generations to come.**
We have an extraordinary opportunity ahead of us. In 2027 and 2028, we can defend the majorities we just won, elect even more Democratic pro-choice women, and continue pushing back against the Republican agenda that has threatened our rights and freedoms for far too long.

President Trump’s plan to rig the midterm elections didn’t just fail — it went up in flames. After redrawing maps that would give them an advantage in 15 more House districts, Republicans thought their House majority was all but guaranteed.
**The opposite happened.** Democratic candidates defeated them in all but three seats they gerrymandered. And California’s responsive effort to level the playing field — made possible by the voters — flipped the redistricting scheme upside down.
Every single person in this movement played a role in helping ensure that the Republican power grab backfired. Whether you signed a petition, donated, contacted your lawmaker, or just talked about this nerdy political issue with your friends, it all paid off.
The American people didn’t just reject Republicans in this election — they rejected their underhanded, cynical scheme to try to rig the results before a single voter had cast a ballot.
Now, as we look toward the future, the NDRC is preparing for the next round of the redistricting crisis. We expect Republicans to respond to these results by doubling down on mid-decade gerrymanders. Lawmakers in Mississippi are already planning to redraw their state legislative and supreme court maps mid-decade. And we’re keeping an eye on Georgia and Texas — states that could redraw their maps in the month and a half before Democrats take power.
**We’re raising the resources now to ensure we can respond immediately to new maps — whether it’s our mapping team’s rapid analysis to help stakeholders understand the implications of redraws or our advocacy and communications teams working to educate the media and voters about what’s at stake. By now you have probably seen the posts. Israel is safer today than it has ever been. Trump wiped out Hamas. Trump wiped out Hezbollah. He even replaced Lloyd's of London -- the insurance market that has underwritten the world's ships for nearly three and a half centuries -- with a new American insurer, overnight. It is a great story. It has a victor, a vanquished, and a toppled British institution, all in a single meme.
It is also three claims that fall apart the moment you hold them up against the actual record. The record matters, because the distance between what we say we won and what we have actually won is precisely where the next war starts...

| | | Peter,
---
My grandpa served in the U.S. Army, and I believe we owe no greater debt than to those who have worn our country’s uniform.
This month, we honored our veterans on Veterans Day. But I’m committed to thanking them for their service with action every day of the year.
| | | [](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/143802114/661414676/1093978781?refcode=BLU_EM_JRFC_2026-11-20_01&amount=25&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMzEvMS85Mzg5MSIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJlOTBiMWY0YS0zZGU1LWYxMTEtOTFmMy0wMDBkM2E1MzM5NzgiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=qm0DY7nBlVezF5ab6Xbt9e3I5as1zviQzFJ4s_ughek=)
---
| | | **That’s why I’m proud to share that the Major Richard Star Act, which I co-sponsored to ensure combat-disabled veterans receive the full benefits they’ve earned, has passed the House!**
---
It builds on the work I’ve been leading in Congress on behalf of Upstate veterans and their families. I’m backing the bipartisan Major Richard Star Act to end the “wounded warrior tax,” which prevents combat-disabled veterans from receiving both their full retirement pay and disability benefits. I’ve also fought to cut VA wait times and expand dental and hearing care for every veteran enrolled in the VA.
As costs rise across the board, these benefits make a real difference for families here at home. We have a responsibility to make sure our veterans get the support they deserve, and I’ll keep fighting for them every single day.
With gratitude & high hopes,
Josh

body:
Winning was step one. Now our job is to turn that win into real action.
# [](https://act.pramilaforcongress.com/go/892?refcode=em20261120-6974-footer&t=1&akid=6974%2E420207%2E0hyN30)
Hi Peter, Pramila Jayapal here.
On November 3rd, we didn’t just win. We won big. We flipped the House, we flipped the Senate, and we won in states that Democrats haven’t carried in decades.
That’s what a people-powered movement looks like, and you helped build it.
**Now, we have to meet _this_ moment. So on Sunday, December 6th, I’m leading a special Resistance Lab, joined by some very special guests: Representative-elect Randy Villegas and Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed. And I want you there, too! [Will you RSVP today to save your spot?](https://act.pramilaforcongress.com/go/55567?utm_source=em20261120-6974&t=2&akid=6974%2E420207%2E0hyN30)**
[](https://act.pramilaforcongress.com/go/55567?utm_source=em20261120-6974&t=3&akid=6974%2E420207%2E0hyN30)
**[RSVP](https://act.pramilaforcongress.com/go/55567?utm_source=em20261120-6974&t=4&akid=6974%2E420207%2E0hyN30)**
Winning was step one. Now our job is to turn that win into real action on Medicare For All, a living wage, an end to ICE cruelty, and more. And it’s going to take organized, engaged people holding their leaders accountable.
After this Resistance lab, you’ll leave with a toolkit for moving forward as our newly-elected leaders are sworn in so that we can continue organizing both on the inside and the outside of the halls of power to accomplish our goals.
[**RSVP today and secure your spot. We’ll send you the Zoom link closer to the event date!**](https://act.pramilaforcongress.com/go/55567?utm_source=em20261120-6974&t=5&akid=6974%2E420207%2E0hyN30)
I hope to see you there,
Pramila Jayapal
